mcqs.question: How does rearranging prefix[j] - prefix[i] = K into prefix[i] = prefix[j] - K enable an O(n) solution for Subarray Sum Equals K?
options: It turns "does a valid subarray end here" into "has this specific prefix-sum value already been seen," which a hashmap answers in O(1)
It requires sorting all prefix sums before scanning the array
It only works when every element in the array is positive
It replaces the hashmap with a two-pointer scan over prefix sums
mcqs.explanation: The rearranged identity is exactly a complement-lookup: the value that would complete a valid subarray becomes a hashmap key to check, avoiding any nested loop over index pairs. No sorting or positivity constraint is required, and no two-pointer scan is involved.

mcqs.question: In the one-pass Subarray Sum Equals K solution, why does the code look up the complement in the map before recording the current running sum?
options: Recording before looking up produces faster runtime by amortizing map inserts
The order doesn't affect correctness, only raw performance
Looking up after recording is required to correctly seed the map with the value 0
Looking up before recording ensures the map only reflects prefix sums from strictly earlier positions, so a subarray is never matched against its own endpoint
mcqs.explanation: Checking first keeps the map limited to earlier indices only, the same discipline as Two Sum's check-before-insert — matching against the current index itself would produce an invalid, zero-length subarray.

mcqs.question: Why must the prefix-sum map be seeded with {0: 1} before scanning begins in Subarray Sum Equals K?
options: It prevents integer overflow when running sums grow large
Without it, subarrays that start at index 0 have no earlier prefix sum to match against and get silently undercounted
It only matters when the array contains negative numbers
It's needed to make the hashmap's average lookup time O(1)
mcqs.explanation: A subarray starting at index 0 needs to match against the sum of an empty prefix, which is 0 by definition — without seeding that value, the lookup finds nothing even when a valid subarray genuinely starts at the beginning.

mcqs.question: Why does the same prefix-sum-plus-hashmap shape work for counting subarrays with a target XOR, not just a target sum?
options: XOR-based counting requires sorting the prefix values first
The XOR variant only works if every element in the array is zero or one
Because XOR is its own inverse (a XOR a = 0), the same "running combine value, then look up what undoes it" shape applies with XOR in place of subtraction
The XOR variant needs a doubly linked list instead of a hashmap
mcqs.explanation: Any running combination with an inverse operation supports this pattern — subtraction undoes addition, and XOR undoes itself — so the same lookup shape carries over unchanged. No sorting, bit restriction, or linked list is involved.

mcqs.question: In the Continuous Subarray Sum (divisible by K) solution, why does the remainder map store only the earliest index seen for each remainder?
options: Because storing every index for a remainder is required for correctness
Because the remainder map must be rebuilt from scratch whenever K changes
Because Python's modulo operator cannot be used with negative running sums
Because keeping only the earliest index maximizes the gap available to satisfy the subarray's minimum-length requirement
mcqs.explanation: A later occurrence of the same remainder would only shrink the gap between matching indices, so keeping the earliest one is strictly at least as good for satisfying a minimum-length check. Correctness doesn't need every index, and this has nothing to do with K changing or Python's modulo behavior.

mcqs.question: Why does a sliding window fail to correctly solve subarray-sum problems once negative numbers are allowed?
options: Because a negative element can shrink the running sum as the window grows, so there's no longer one guaranteed-correct direction to move the window's edges
Because sliding window cannot be implemented in O(n) time at all
Because negative numbers make prefix sums mathematically undefined
Because sliding window requires the array to be sorted first
mcqs.explanation: Sliding window relies on the sum changing monotonically as the window expands or shrinks; negative numbers break that monotonicity, so there's no longer a single safe direction to adjust the window. Prefix sums remain well-defined for negative numbers, and sorting isn't a prerequisite for either technique.
